Hi there, I'm new to Lean and Zulip. I have a question regarding some unexpected behavior in lean around universe level metavariables. Here a minimal example that demonstrates my question:

def testDef : Prop := ∃ (X : Type*), True

def testSet : Set ℕ := {A : ℕ | testDef}

At the second line, I get the error: "declaration testSet contains universe level metavariables at the expression fun A ↦ testDef.{?u.6034} in the declaration body {A | testDef.{?u.6034}}."

But, there is no error when I expand the definition of testDef by writing: def testSetTwo : Set ℕ := {A : ℕ | ∃ (X : Type*), True}

I think I can see why I get the "universe level metavariables" error, though I'm happy to get anyone's take on it. I'd really like to know how I can avoid having to expand the definition manually to avoid the error.

Thanks!

Maybe we should have a linter against this... When you write

import Mathlib

def testDef : Prop := ∃ (X : Type*), True

what that means is

def testDef.{u} : Prop := ∃ (X : Type u), True

i.e. for every universe u, testDef.{u} is defined as ∃ (X : Type u), True, so e.g. testDef.{0} means ∃ (X : Type), True and testDef.{1} means ∃ (X : Type 1), True.
Then when you write testSet, it doesn't know which testDef it should use; testDef.{0} or testDef.{1} or ...? So it complains. The fact is that you can't quantify over universe levels in Lean, so something like ∃ u (X : Type u), True or ∀ u (X : Type u), True is not possible. However, depending on the case, it might be enough to just use Type or some other fixed universe level.

Thanks, @Robin Arnez , for the quick and detailed response. A follow-up would be: Lean doesn't complain when I write
def testSetTwo : Set ℕ := {A : ℕ | ∃ (X : Type*), True}
Is this the same as
def testSetTwo.{u} : Set ℕ := {A : ℕ | ∃ (X : Type u), True}
or can the type differ for different elements of the set?

I have a specific definition in mind in my project where this is causing problems. But I'd like to understand what's going on here before getting into that, in the hopes that I might be able to solve it myself : )

or can the type differ for different elements of the set?

Just make the definition yourself and #print it to see!

Since I don't see it explicitly spelled out above, you can fix your error (but perhaps not your intent) with

def testSet.{u} : Set ℕ := {A : ℕ | testDef.{u}}

Thanks, Kevin and Eric. I see by #print that that indeed
def testSetTwo : Set ℕ := {A : ℕ | ∃ (X : Type*), True}
is the same as
def testSetTwo.{u} : Set ℕ := {A : ℕ | ∃ (X : Type u), True}
So, Eric's suggestion is a way around unfolding the definition from my first post.

I have to ask another question to determine whether this solves my problem. Suppose I write
'def test : Set ℕ := { n | ∃ (G : Type*) (_ : Group G), ... }'
I know now that this means
'def test.{u} : Set ℕ := { n | ∃ (G : Type u) (_ : Group G), ... }'
so that test is a function of the universe.

Is there a universe u that "contains all groups", in the sense that test.{u} will return what I mean when I write in English: {n \in N | there exists a group G such that ...}? This questions extends more broadly: is there a universe that "contains all (mathematical object I want to quantify over)" in this same sense?
well test.{u} means something like "there exists a group of size <=u such that..."
you can make pretty much any construction you want in Type 0 except for quantifying over Type 0 itself
in Type 1 you can do all that again but you can also quantify over Type 0, and then in Type 2 you can quantify over Type 1 as well, and then...

Is there a universe u that "contains all groups", in the sense that test.{u} will return what I mean when I write in English: {n \in N | there exists a group G such that ...}?

Yes: Type contains all groups (in the sense that group theorists mean when they talk about groups).

These higher universes are just an artefact of Lean's type theory -- everything has to have a type, even things like the collection of all sets, so you end up with these absurdly large things which are convenient in a technical sense but not relevant to most everyday mathematics.
Presumably you could consider Units (Cardinal.{0}) as a group that lives in Type 1, but no typical mathematician would?

That's the trivial group so it's isomorphic to (but not equal to) a group living in Type. But the point is that when a mathematician says "group", either they're talking about a group in Type (99.9% of the time) or they're doing something fairly obscure involving things which aren't sets (like Cardinal.{0}, the class of all cardinals) and will know all about universes anyway.

There is no way in Lean to quantify over all universes.

Daniel Glasscock said:

Is there a universe u that "contains all groups", in the sense that test.{u} will return what I mean when I write in English: {n \in N | there exists a group G such that ...}? This questions extends more broadly: is there a universe that "contains all (mathematical object I want to quantify over)" in this same sense?

This seems like an #xy. You usually do not want to quantify over types like this. What are you trying to do?

Oh I don't think that's true. It's perfectly reasonable to ask questions about e.g. the set of natural numbers N such that there exists a simple group of order N, or the N for which there exists a group generated by N elements with some property etc etc

Wow, I appreciate all the discussion. I have to be honest that I'm uneasy about the direction this is headed, and not just because I'm not a set theorist... I'm concerned that verifying results that we accept as stated in English may require an extra step.

More precisely: say I want to verify in Lean the theorem "{n \in \N | there exists a group G such that ...} = set of even positive integers".If I get a proof in Lean of {n : ℕ | ∃ (G : Type) (_ : Group G), ... } = {n : ℕ | Even n}, then does this serve as verification? Or, as has been suggested, would I need to provide extra assurance that there is not an "esoteric" group living outside of Type (who knows, maybe I'm not a "typical" mathematician?) which demonstrates that some odd positive integer n belongs to the set?

You can split it into two parts: One part that says that for every group such that ... n is even and then an explicit construction of such a group for every even n as a definition + group instance declaration + lemma and then you can write a proof of {n : ℕ | ∃ (G : Type) (_ : Group G), ... } = {n : ℕ | Even n} as a corollary of those two facts.

I think this is basically what Robin is saying but let me give an example which is already in mathlib:
In the subject of Model Theory, a theory (a set of sentences in First order logic) is Satisfiable iff there exists some model of it.
The standard set theory definition existentially quantifies over all possible Models (i.e. all possible domains a model might take).
In Lean we cannot do this unbounded quantification, we can only quantify up to some big-enough universe level - which we need to pick in the definition.
But (at least in this situation) we can prove that any bigger universe level, wouldn't have changed the meaning of our original definition.
In more explicit terms lets look at
https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/8850ed93863d6ce27210a673f9ed235a4e8a2994/Mathlib/ModelTheory/Satisfiability.lean#L64-L66

It defines a theory T to be Satisfiable iff there exists a model with domain in Type (max u v), where u and v are the universe parameters from the type of variables and the type of symbols used in the first order language L - i.e. Type (max u v) is the smallest universe level containing all the syntactic symbols. (L is an implicit argument of the definition, coming from the variable command above.. so all universes in that definition come are mentioned in arguments, i.e. the definition has no free universe parameters, which is very nice)

Now, why is this a faithful formalization of satisfiability?
A few lines below there is a Theorem Model.isSatisfiable that says:
Given any model of a theory T (with domain in a completely arbitrary universe Type w that is a free parameter of the theorem)
there exists a model of T with domain in Type (max u v), i.e. T is Satisfiable by the definition of earlier.

But proving this second part is of course real work and i don't know enough about the metatheory of Lean to assert that one can always pick a large-enough universe parameter in the definition and then prove that any at-least-as-large universe parameter (in the sense of max of universes) would have given the same definition

One additional thing to consider (which is currently not done in mathlib) is to make the definition of Satisfiable public but non-exposed - only expose that Satisfiable -> ex. model with domain in Type (max u v) and expose
ex. model with any universe parameter -> Satisfiable to remove the footgun of a user trying to prove Satisfiable from the definition and then getting a hard to diagnose universe mismatch because his provided model is not in the right universe

Daniel Glasscock ha dicho:

More precisely: say I want to verify in Lean the theorem "{n \in \N | there exists a group G such that ...} = set of even positive integers".If I get a proof in Lean of {n : ℕ | ∃ (G : Type) (_ : Group G), ... } = {n : ℕ | Even n}, then does this serve as verification? Or, as has been suggested, would I need to provide extra assurance that there is not an "esoteric" group living outside of Type (who knows, maybe I'm not a "typical" mathematician?) which demonstrates that some odd positive integer n belongs to the set?

Unless your esoteric structure looks like a strongly inaccessible cardinal there's little reason for concern. Proper classes/larger universes are by and large just more of the same.

So e.g. if you're talking about a finite group, that's not a problem, those are "all the same" across universes. This also applies to countable groups, or groups with cardinality ≤ 𝔠, or really any structure whose cardinal is less than docs#Cardinal.univ (i.e. everything you know and love with like three exceptions).

And even if that's not the case, very little changes. There's very few results in mathematics that crucially depend on whether there's provably at least one strongly inaccessible cardinal smaller than the structure you're working with.
(And those that do usually require something stronger, like a stationary set of inaccessibles, so universes don't do much for you either)

Kevin Buzzard said:

Oh I don't think that's true. It's perfectly reasonable to ask questions about e.g. the set of natural numbers N such that there exists a simple group of order N, or the N for which there exists a group generated by N elements with some property etc etc

These are all small properties which can be done with quantification over small things (e.g. group structures over Fin n, or normal subgroups of FreeGroup (Fin n))

Daniel Glasscock said:

More precisely: say I want to verify in Lean the theorem "{n \in \N | there exists a group G such that ...} = set of even positive integers".If I get a proof in Lean of {n : ℕ | ∃ (G : Type) (_ : Group G), ... } = {n : ℕ | Even n}, then does this serve as verification?

Yes.

Actually no, but only because 0 is a natural in Lean, so {n : ℕ | Even n} is the set of even nonnegative integers. Other than that, yes.
It is worth mentioning that unless something very weird is going on, if your proof works for Type 0, it should almost certainly work for Type u.

the first way says "even even number generates a group for which ..."
for this direction the group should be in Type

I think this is ultimately what I'm concerned with. Apparently a proof of {n : ℕ | ∃ (G : Type) (_ : Group G), ... } = {n : ℕ | Even n} in Lean by itself may not convince the skeptic that "{n \in \N | there exists a group G such that ...} = set of evennon-negative integers". It seems it is more difficult to translate between Lean code and math english than I originally thought!

There have been two suggested approaches: @Moritz R suggests coupling it an argument that Type is sufficient, and @Robin Arnez / @Aaron Liu suggest proving it as two statements. Both sound good to me.

Violeta Hernández said:

There is no way in Lean to quantify over all universes.

Is it true that you cannot quantify over all universe levels though? Something like

∀ u, {U : Type u} -> _

Or even over the universe levels currently in play?
You can only quantify over universes in a very restricted way, which is by having your definitions and theorems be universe polymorphic
that is the only was you can quantify over universes, there is no way to do it otherwise
in particular, you cannot have a theorem that says "exists a universe u, ...", and you cannot have a theorem taking an assumption "forall universes u, ..."

Aaron Liu said:

Yes, and afaik for universe polymorphic definitions one should really think of this as a separate definition per universe - not as a quantification on universes!
Please correct me if you think otherwise, im really not an expert on type systems
I wonder, can one formulate a universe polymorphic definition in Lean and even prove in Lean that it behaves differently for at least 2 different universes?
I feel like one might be able to use Prop and proof irrelevancy for this
My feeling is that for non-prop universes the proving in Lean part is probably impossible?

Yes you can do this with stupid definitions. The natural numbers such that there exists a group in Type u which isn't isomorphic to any group in Type is no natural numbers for u=0 and all natural numbers for u>0.

For the original poster I think it's important to stress that the answer to their question is clear: just use Type and that's the end of it. These foundational questions are of interest but they're nothing to do with the original question.
What is the witness group here which lives in Type 1 but is not isomorphic to anything in Type?
(im just curious)
How about the free group on Type?
Oh right, that exists
docs#Cardinal.IsInaccessible is a universe polymorphic definition, for which you can find examples in universes u>0, but it is consistent that there are no examples in universe u=0

When using Lean you are assuming "different axioms" than ZFC (well really, it is a completely different - but also somehow related - system of logic + axioms). Looking at this very interesting stackexchange
and this Zulip discussion, it is (at least currently) unclear how to exactly connect theorems in Lean to theorems in ZFC.

To me it sounds like you are essentially argueing:
"The Statement for Type 0 corresponds to the statement in ZFC, so this is what should be proven"

But i think the linked discussions are arguing that this correspondence really is extremely subtle if it even exists.

In my mind the only really safe route to go is
Prove the statement for a free universe variable since that is the "most strong"? way to formulate a non-existence statement in Lean - but it also is more work than the Type 0 version.

There are two completely different discussions going on in this thread.

1) There is "I am a beginner who doesn't care about set theory and am trying to write a basic question in group theory, how do I solve the problem posted at the beginning of this thread", to which the answer is "use Type".

2) There is "I am very interested in foundations and the consequences of using Type instead of Type u" and you can talk about those things for as long as you like. And the more you talk about them, the more you confuse the beginner.

What im saying is, when formalizing in Lean you must do a choice, and what im saying is that the choice does matter. And you seem to have made a choice, but haven't given any arguments on why your choice is "the correct one" in your point of view.

I totally agree that Type and Type u give different answers. The reason Type is the right answer for the OP is that when they eventually explained their question several posts later, Type was the right answer.
(but why is it the right answer..?)

Becuse when a mathematician who is not interested in foundations and who thinks they're working in ZFC says "the natural numbers n such that there exists a group such that...", they mean "the natural numbers n such that there exists a group in Type such that...".

I would argue that this is not always the case. For example, if I want "the set of natural numbers n such that there exists an R-module of rank n", then I should not be quantifying over Type, but instead whatever universe R is in.

I totally agree that if there are other universes involved then it becomes more complicated. But when the OP clarified their question this was not the case.

All I am saying is that for the specific question which the OP asked, Type is the right answer. I absolutely agree that for more general classes of questions the answer is more complicated (we are all in complete agreement on this) and I am despairing about how people want to make this thread more complicated and want to scare the beginner off.
